# Lohicca Sutta (DN 12 (PTS DN i 224))

**ID:** DN 12 (PTS DN i 224)
**Section:** Dīghanikāya (dn)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Lohicca Sutta
**PTS:** DN i 224
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0101m.mul11.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Lohicca Sutta* (DN 12) is the twelfth discourse of the *Dīghanikāya* and belongs to the *Sīlakkhandhavagga* [Gethin 2001; Hazra 1994]. Set at Sālavatikā—a royal domain under King Pasenadi of Kosala granted to the brahmin Lohicca—the discourse centers on Lohicca's pernicious view (*pāpakaṁ diṭṭhigataṁ*) that an ascetic or brahmin who has attained a wholesome doctrine should not teach it to others [Walshe 1987; Jennings 1948; Seeger 2005]. Lohicca reasoned that one person cannot do anything for another, comparing the declaration of the doctrine to binding a new fetter after cutting an old one [Walshe 1987; Seeger 2005; Shih You Xin 2009]. After Lohicca sends his barber Bhesika to invite the Buddha for a meal, the Buddha visits his residence and engages him in a dialogue on the ethics of teaching [Walshe 1987; Allon 1997; Humphreys 1956]. The Buddha refutes Lohicca's reasoning with analogies, showing that a teacher withholding instruction acts destructively toward prospective disciples, and delineates three types of blameworthy teachers in contrast to blameless teachers [Humphreys 1956; Hazra 1994; Shih You Xin 2009]. The sutta then rehearses the standard sequential path of training and spiritual attainments shared with the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta* (DN 2), though without explicitly dividing it into three separate categories [Gethin 2001; Hazra 1994; Gethin 2008].

 The text is also cited in the *Mahāniddesa* (Mnd 14) and *Kathāvatthu* (Kv 10.3, Kv 18.9).

**Sources**

- [Gethin 2001] R. M. Gethin, The Buddhist Path to Awakening (2001) — Identified the structure of the Sīlakkhandhavagga path account in DN 12.
- [Humphreys 1956] Christmas Humphreys (ed.), Buddhist Students Manual (1956) — Subject matter of the dialogue with Lohicca on the ethics of teaching.
- [Walshe 1987] Maurice Walshe, The Long Discourses of the Buddha: A Translation of the Dīgha Nikāya (1987) — Narrative setting at Sālavatikā, Lohicca's view and analogy of the fetter, and the dispatch of the barber Bhesika.
- [Hazra 1994] Kanai Lal Hazra, Pāli Language and Literature (1994) — Summary of the discussion on blameworthy and blameless teachers and reuse of Sāmaññaphala material.
- [Seeger 2005] Martin Seeger, Phra Dhammapiṭaka und die Pāli-Kanon-Debatte in Thailand (2005) — Pali phrasing of Lohicca's wrong view and the Buddha's refutation through dialogue.
- [Gethin 2008] Rupert Gethin, Sayings of the Buddha (2008) — Comparison of the fruits of ascetic life scheme in DN 12.
- [Shih You Xin 2009] Lim Hwee San (Shih You Xin), Study of the Connotation, Significance and Development of Resolve in Early Buddhism (2009) — Buddha's use of analogies to demonstrate danger to disciples when teachers withhold instruction.
- [Allon 1997] Mark Allon, Style and Function (1997) — Formulaic features: the barber Bhesika acting as messenger, approach formulas, and the post-meal dialogue resulting in conversion.
- [Jennings 1948] James George Jennings, The Vedāntic Buddhism of the Buddha (1948) — Note on King Pasenadi's jurisdiction over Lohicca's estate in the Lohikka Sutta (DN 12).
